name: Instatus
summary: Hosted status pages that tell customers about outages and maintenance, with built-in uptime monitors that can open incidents, and on-call schedules for the team behind them.
intro: Instatus started as a cheaper, faster status page and is still built around one. You list your components (API, dashboard, payments), group them, and post incidents and scheduled maintenance with updates as they progress. Subscribers hear about each update by email, SMS, webhook, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Google Chat or RSS, and a public API lets customers pull your status into their own tools. Pages can be public, private behind a login, or on your own domain, and third-party components show the status of services you depend on, such as AWS or Stripe, so customers can see when a problem is upstream.

Monitoring came later. Website, API, cron heartbeat, ping, TCP, UDP and DNS monitors check from one location at a time, rotating between the United States, Canada, Europe and Asia; when one fails or recovers, Instatus can open or resolve an incident, publish it to the page and notify subscribers. Alerts from other tools, such as Datadog, can drive incidents through a webhook. For the team, on-call schedules with rotations, escalation policies and routing rules decide who gets the email, SMS or phone call. A REST API at `api.instatus.com` covers pages, components, incidents, monitors and subscribers. The free Starter plan includes 15 monitors at 2-minute intervals and 200 subscribers; Pro starts at $20 a month.
strengths: A full status page with incidents, maintenance windows, private pages and many subscriber channels on a free plan

Cheaper than Statuspage for the same audience: Pro, from $20 a month, covers 5,000 subscribers and 50 team members, where Statuspage’s Business plan charges $300 a month for 5,000 subscribers and 25 team members
Monitors, on-call and the status page in one tool, so a failed check can update customers without a human in the loop
Third-party components show customers when the outage is at a provider you depend on
limits: Monitoring is basic next to dedicated synthetics tools: no scripted browser journeys, and each check runs from a single location at a time, so it can’t confirm a failure from several places at once
Closed-source SaaS: the status page is only as available as Instatus itself, and there is no self-hosted version
Plan limits on subscribers (200 free, 5,000 on Pro) and on-call members push larger audiences to Business or Enterprise
SAML single sign-on needs the Business plan, and SCIM, multiple SSO connections and an uptime SLA need Enterprise

worksWith.how: opens and resolves incidents from alerts in

story: Ali Salah, a developer from Cairo, quit his job and started Instatus in June 2019. The market leader was Atlassian’s Statuspage, which tiers its plans by subscribers and team members. By 2020 Instatus pitched itself directly against it: a status page in 10 seconds, “10x faster to load than Statuspage”, at under 5% of the price, with unlimited teammates and subscribers on a flat $20-a-month Pro plan.

The speed claim came from architecture. Instatus called itself a Jamstack status page: each page was static, regenerated within seconds of an update and served independently of any backend, so it stayed up when the customer’s own systems and Instatus’s app did not. Monitoring was left to others, with integrations for Pingdom, New Relic, UptimeRobot, Runscope, Freshping and Datadog.

Salah ran Instatus as a small, founder-led company; by late 2022 he reported about $10,000 in monthly recurring revenue and more than 350 paying customers. Instatus then added its own monitors, on-call schedules and escalation, turning the status page into a small incident-response product.

choices.why: A status page must be up when everything else is down. Generating static pages that load without a backend made them fast and independent of Instatus’s own app.

choices.choice: Flat pricing with unlimited teammates and subscribers
choices.why: Statuspage tiers its prices by subscribers and team members, so one flat price with no such limits was the clearest way to win small teams. Today’s Instatus plans do cap both, at higher numbers.

choices.choice: Integrate with monitors first, build them later
choices.why: Early Instatus took alerts from existing monitoring services; built-in monitors and on-call came later so smaller teams could use one tool.
